title: Susan Gough's psychological operations role as a source for the WSJ article
place_text: Booz Allen Hamilton / Department of Defense, USA

tellings.quote: One of the articles primary sources is Susan Gough, whose own LinkedIn, along with independent sources, confirms her lead role in Booz Allen Hamilton's Psychological Operations Consulting Practice for the Department of Defense.

In a statement, a Defense Department spokeswoman acknowledged that AARO had uncovered evidence of fake classified program materials relating to extraterrestrials, and had briefed lawmakers and intelligence officials.

The spokeswoman, Sue Gough, said the department didn’t include that information in its report last year because the investigation wasn’t completed, but expects to provide it in another report scheduled for later this year.

plain: Michels argues that a 2025 Wall Street Journal article dismissing UFO stories leaned on a source with a background in military psychological operations. The article, "The Pentagon Disinformation That Fueled America's UFO Mythology," was written by Joel Schectman and published on 6 June 2025. It argues that some UFO lore grew out of Pentagon deception. Michels says that "one of the articles primary sources is Susan Gough." He adds that her LinkedIn profile and other sources confirm "her lead role in Booz Allen Hamilton's Psychological Operations Consulting Practice for the Department of Defense," Booz Allen Hamilton being a large defense consulting firm. The article itself quotes Gough once, as a Defense Department spokeswoman. In that statement she confirms that AARO, the Pentagon's current office for investigating unexplained sightings, "had uncovered evidence of fake classified program materials relating to extraterrestrials," and says this will be reported later that year. For the rest, the article cites "interviews with two dozen current and former U.S. officials, scientists and military contractors" whom it does not name. Whether Gough shaped the article beyond that one statement, the article does not say, and it says nothing about her career. Michels's point is that if she did, the piece may itself have been a form of influence.

discussion.by: The Pentagon Disinformation That Fueled America's UFO Mythology (The Wall Street Journal, 2025)
discussion.text: The article quotes Sue Gough once, as the Defense Department spokeswoman whose statement confirms that AARO "had uncovered evidence of fake classified program materials relating to extraterrestrials" and that the department expects to report it later; it says the rest of its account rests on "interviews with two dozen current and former U.S. officials, scientists and military contractors involved in the inquiry" without naming them. Gough as one of the article's primary sources is the teller's reading of her role beyond that statement, and the article says nothing of her career.
